newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole slug it out in spirited first debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole slug it out in spirited first debate.

text.p: Republican presidential challenger Bob Dole attacked President Bill Clinton on foreign policy, drugs, the economy and his own credibilty and drew heavy return fire in a spirited, sometimes heated first debate of the campaign.

Standing a few feet apart behind lecterns that looked, fittingly, like pulpits on a stage carpeted in blood red, the two candidates hammered at each other in a 90-minute encounter that saw underdog Dole take the offensive and Clinton coolly parrying him in a series of sharp exchanges.

"We are better off than we were four years ago. Let's keep it going," Clinton said at the outset in trying to stake out ground clearly safe and defensible for a candidate 15 to 20 points up in the polls less than a month before the Nov. 5 election day.
"Well, he's better off than he was four years ago," Dole said of Clinton, getting one of many laughs he provoked from the Bushnell Theatre audience with one liners.
He asserted that a few may be better off but that "the American people are working harder and paying more taxes."

All sides agreed Dole had to score some major breakthrough in this huge televised forum and he tried to do it -- while avoiding the reputation for bitterness that has dogged him for years -- by repeatedly attacking Clinton's policies and taking shots at his character. Clinton seemed largely unflustered.

Typical of the cut and thrust was a Dole demand, near the end of the encounter, that Clinton say clearly whether he meant to pardon any of his former Arkansas colleagues recently convicted of fraud in business dealings related to the Whitewater land deal that had dogged Clinton himself.
Clinton replied affably that "there's been no consideration of it and no discussion of it ... I will adhere to the law."

In another effort to rattle Clinton with personal shots, Dole suggested the president was constantly exaggerating the credit he deserves for America's economic prosperity and successes in preserving peace.

"You know the president reminds me of my brother Kenny who is no longer alive," Dole said with a grin. "Kenny was a great talker. And he used to tell me things that were not quite accurate, so we always divided by six. Now maybe in your case, maybe just two," he said to Clinton, who shrugged it off.

Even so, tempers were always controlled, the two men admitted to liking and respecting each other, and at the end the two shook hands warmly and posed on stage with their smiling families gathered alongside as the crowd applauded.
Two instant public opinion polls by ABC and CBS television networks suggested Clinton was the winner.

Missing from the encounter was Ross Perot, the Texas billionaire and Reform Party presidential candidate who enlivened the debates four years ago but was excluded this year by agreement of Dole, Clinton and the debate commission.
No news was made of policy matters but the two covered the horizon, prodded along by debate moderator Jim Lehrer, a public television news anchor who was the sole questioner.

On foreign policy, Dole said he was "disappointed" at the lack of progress and hasty nature of the two-day Middle East crisis summit Clinton hosted last week in an effort to stop Israeli-Palestinian violence.
"It's almost like an ad hoc foreign policy," Dole said."It's ad hoc, sort of like you get up in the morning and read the papers and see what country's in trouble, and we'll have a meeting."

Clinton replied: "I would like to have had a big organised summit but those people were killing each other ... I felt that if I could just get the parties together to say let's stop the violence, start talking, commit to negotiations, that would be a plus."

To Dole's charges that he had "deployed more troops than any president in history around the world" and undermined U.S. credibility, Clinton noted that peace however fragile still prevailed in trouble spots like Bosnia and the Middle East.
He also cited his efforts in Haiti and Northern Ireland as showing he has maintained the U.S. leadership role.
Dole said the centrepiece of Clinton's 1993 economic plan that the president says restored the U.S. economy included a tax increase that raised taxes on all Americans, not just the wealthy.
Clinton said Dole acknowledged earlier this year that the American economy is in its best shape in 30 years, but Dole said he doubted having said that.
Dole also accused Clinton on drug abuse and special interest money, drawing rebukes from his rival each time.

"When you're a few million short, you run out to Hollywood and pick up 2 to 4 million (dollars), and organised labour comes to Washington and puts 35 million (dollars) into the pot," Dole said on the special interest issue and the need for campaign finance reform.

"Senator Dole's had some pretty harsh comments on special interests recently," Clinton replied, "but it wasn't me who opposed what we tried to do to save the lives of children who were subject to tobacco and then went to the tobacco growers and bragged about standing up to the government when we tried to stop the advertising, marketing and sales of tobacco to children."

The face-to-face meeting was the first of two presidential debates between Democratic Clinton and Dole. A vice presidential debate between Democratic incumbent Al Gore and Dole's running mate Jack Kemp is scheduled for Wednesday, while Dole and Clinton have a followup on Oct. 16.
